conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply 10 questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. Your answers stay between you and our care team, and there are no right or wrong responses—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can pause anytime.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first one:

Over the past week, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that been pretty hard to do?

[soft sigh]  
Honestly… most days it feels really hard. My husband will try to make a joke—something that used to make me crack up—and I just stare at him. I might force a little smile so he doesn’t worry, but inside I feel flat, like nothing’s funny anymore. I did laugh once, when my older niece sent a silly video, but it faded fast and I felt guilty for even enjoying it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow head-shake]  
Not really… I mean, I’ve managed a couple of half-smiles when my husband tried to be funny, but it feels forced. Most of the time nothing seems funny at all.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet shrug]

I haven’t really looked forward to much of anything lately. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now when I think of doing them it just feels… empty, like “what’s the point?” I still go, mainly so people won’t worry, but there’s no spark beforehand and barely any pleasure once I’m there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes drop to the floor]

Yeah... that happens a lot. If the baby spits up more than usual or won’t settle, my head jumps straight to "I must be doing something wrong." Yesterday I cried because I couldn’t get her to nap—kept thinking, "A good mom would know the trick." Even little stuff like forgetting to switch the laundry makes me feel I’m failing. I know in my head it’s not all on me, but the guilty voice keeps saying I should be better at this.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes... pretty much every day. I'll be feeding her and suddenly my heart starts racing—like, what if she chokes, what if her breathing sounds different, what if I'm not making enough milk for her? Nothing's actually wrong, but I can't shake the dread. Sometimes I catch myself staring at the baby monitor for ages just to be sure she's okay. After a while I can usually calm down, but it keeps coming back out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[wrings hands in lap]

A few times, yeah. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, heart races, and I think something awful is about to happen even though I can’t name what. Last night I was rocking the baby in the dark and felt that rush; I had to put her in the crib a minute so I could sit and breathe. It passes after a bit, but it leaves me shaky and embarrassed.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales slowly]

Most days, honestly. Between the night feeds, the piles of laundry, and trying to keep the baby content, it feels like I’m drowning in small tasks. I’ll start one thing, hear her cry, drop everything, and by evening nothing’s finished and I’m exhausted. I keep telling myself other moms manage, so why can’t I? It’s overwhelming, but I still get the essentials done—just barely.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quiet voice, eyes tired]

Yeah… I lie down and my head just spins with all the “what-ifs” about the baby, or I replay every little thing I think I messed up. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and when she finally dozes I jerk awake, sure I heard her cry. Even when I do sleep it’s thin and restless; I wake up feeling like I never really rested.
I have felt sad or miserable

[nods slowly, eyes glassy]

Pretty much every day. There’s this heavy sadness that sits on my chest from the moment I open my eyes. I’ll look at the baby and feel like I should be glowing, but instead I just feel empty or like I want to cry. Some afternoons I end up sobbing while I rock her, thinking I’m failing her even though she’s peacefully asleep.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah... that’s been happening. I’ll be folding her tiny clothes or just looking at her sleeping and tears start pouring out. Sometimes it’s because I feel overwhelmed, sometimes I don’t even know why—just this heavy sadness that won’t lift. It’s probably three or four times this week.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—never. I might feel low and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby deserves.

You've shared how, day after day, post-birth joy feels out of reach-laughter is forced, simple pleasures seem pointless, and an unshakeable heaviness follows you from the first morning feed to the final night-time check. Waves of worry about your baby's safety race through your mind, sudden panicky surges make your chest tighten, and nightly rumination keeps you from restful sleep. Yet you've stayed devoted to your little one, pushing through tears, self-blame, and exhaustion while protecting both of you from any thought of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no ability to laugh; responses are forced and nothing feels funny, aligning with "Not at all".</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, pervasive self-blame ('that happens a lot,' 'kept thinking I should be better'), matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, intrusive, irrational worries with physical anxiety symptoms and compulsive checking, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses sudden waves of panic with physical symptoms "a few times" in the past week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm and difficulty managing tasks, aligning with "sometimes haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, nearly nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep directly linked to unhappiness and intrusive thoughts</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness, emptiness, frequent crying, and feelings of failure—clearly matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes crying episodes 3-4 times in the past week triggered by overwhelming sadness, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 24 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> requiring prompt evaluation. You endorse ≥5 key symptoms consistent with <med>DSM-5 Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest/pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, recurrent anxiety/panic, and insomnia. Your description of <quote>heavy sadness that sits on my chest</quote> and <quote>nothing seems funny anymore</quote> illustrates pervasive anhedonia and low mood, while <quote>I must be doing something wrong</quote> reflects disproportionate self-reproach. Daily somatic anxiety, intrusive worries, and nocturnal hypervigilance suggest co-occurring <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. Absence of self-harm ideation is protective, yet severity and functional impairment warrant urgent assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Involve a trusted adult to help with night feeds or household tasks so you can obtain 4-5 hour stretches of sleep
4. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track response to interventions
5. Call 988 or local emergency services immediately if thoughts of self-harm ever emerge
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant age not specified)  
Date: [today’s date]  
Screener: [name], LMHP  

A. Relevant Symptoms / Behaviors Reported  
- Anhedonia: marked loss of pleasure/interest in usual activities; laughter feels “forced”  
- Persistent low mood, “heavy sadness,” tearfulness 3–4×/week (often unprovoked)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt (“I’m failing,” “a good mom would know”)  
- Daily, uncontrollable worries about infant safety; somatic anxiety (racing heart, chest tightness)  
- Discrete panic episodes (“wave,” shakiness, no clear trigger)  
- Sleep disturbance: initial insomnia, restless/“thin” sleep despite infant resting  
- Subjective sense of being “drowning in tasks,” difficulty completing routine chores  
- No suicidal ideation or self-harm thoughts endorsed (denied)  

B. Pattern Summary  
Answers consistently reflect low mood, anhedonia, anxiety, and functional overwhelm beginning post-delivery; symptoms present “pretty much every day” and interfere with sleep, task completion, and emotional bonding.  

C. Screening Significance  
- Edinburgh score likely in moderate–high range (formal scoring pending)  
- Meets DSM-5-TR screening criteria for Major Depressive Episode (≥5 symptoms) and probable comorbid anxiety disorder  
- Denial of self-harm lowers immediate safety risk but continued monitoring indicated  

D. Recommendations (for chart, not treatment)  
1. Complete EPDS for quantified score; review prior to leaving clinic  
2. Consider referral to OB/postpartum psychiatry and/or individual therapy for further evaluation and possible evidence-based treatment  
3. Provide psycho-education on postpartum mood/anxiety disorders; encourage support system activation  
4. Schedule follow-up within 1–2 weeks; instruct to seek immediate care if suicidal thoughts develop  

[End of screening note]
